They were not just tank lorries. They were also refrigerator lorries carrying meat, and there were trucks carrying weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But if we can call this a convoy or a transport, was there permission from the BH army in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: There was, and when we saw that permit, or rather the policemen who were working there saw it, they allowed the trucks with the weapons to pass, but they kept the trucks transporting fuel and food, the reason being that the HVO of Vares had totally prohibited the use of all material resources for the BH army, which means that we couldn't procure a gram of fuel or food. We took advantage of this opportunity to take for ourselves some of the food and fuel and to turn it back to Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So we agree that this was confiscated from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: A part of it. I'm talking about fuel and food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But do you know where the meat ended up? Did it go outside the territory of Vares municipality?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No. The meat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Naumovski, I think that in the cross-examination, since you started, it is almost an hour and a half now. One should go directly to the question. Regarding this particular question of the convoy, go directly to the question, because we can't tell where you're heading. You have twenty different questions, and after a certain amount of time, we are not able to follow. We want to know where you are going. You asked him whether he was aware of that incident. Tell him what it is you want him to tell you, and do it throughout, please, throughout the cross-examination. You are dividing up each question into twenty questions, and in the end, we don't know what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Mahmutovic helped me and gave me the answer that I wanted from him, so let us hurry on. I am watching the time, but it is difficult for me to move quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you spoke about this unit, TO unit, in the area of Stupni Do, would you tell us, were they directly subordinated to you in terms of command?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: For as long as I was the commander of the TO headquarters, the 1st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You told us that the unit numbered some 50 men; some were in uniforms, others in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Husnija Mahmutovic who is mentioned here, he's a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: He's the son of my uncle. We are the children of two brothers; in other words, cousins.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Having mentioned that, the Prosecutor has tendered a document compiled by the European Monitoring Mission, and in that document mention is made of the black market for cigarettes, the smuggling of cigarettes. To follow Judge Bennouna's advice, let me ask you were you aware that cigarettes were being smuggled in that area as a matter of common knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Until when were you the commander of the TO?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 1st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I held a position in the operative group Oganj Visoko attached to the command of the 1st Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: What position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I was an operative officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In the headquarters, in the staff?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the staff, focusing on the tactical group whose assignment was to monitor developments in the area of Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in relation to the fighting in Stupni Do, you said that it was your estimate that some 200 soldiers arrived in the vehicles that you saw, but were all the vehicles full? Were you able to see that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell that they were full, but usually military estimates are made on the basis of the number of vehicles, and one counts the equipment that was being transported, so one makes that estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So may I summarise? It means you made that estimate indirectly, that you came to the conclusion that there was some 200 men?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Before these soldiers arrived in connection with the Stupni Do event, several months before that there were some 500 men who had come from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is in information we received from Vares, and that is why instructions were issued that the civilian population of Stupni Do should be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My question would be, directly, are they the people of Travnik who, through Serb territories and Vlasic, reached this area after the Serb forces had captured Travnik and without any weapons?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they got there, but I do know that they went through Fojnica to Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But my question was were they unarmed?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were armed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that the Muslims who had lived in the village of Dastansko had also been required to surrender their weapons. Did they do that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: What about the inhabitants of Stupni Do; they didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you said that there was some negotiations over the matter. I didn't quite understand what you meant. Were there negotiations on the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: EKREM MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Zvonko Duznovic travelled frequently towards the village of Mir, where there was an HVO unit, the village of Mir, and he travelled there frequently. And passing through Stupni Do or close to Stupni Do, he would say to people providing security of the village that they had to surrender their weapons. They were also called upon, through certain persons from the Przici unit, to come to talks and discuss these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I'm looking at the time. I don't know how long we're planning to work today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's about time that we adjourned. Mr. Naumovski, do you have very much more for this witness, do you think, in order that we can plan tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, you already caught me once in a very poor estimate, so I'm strictly following the chronology of the witness's testimony, and I've covered about two thirds of it. I hope to cover the rest very quickly tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, in view of the fact that you have mentioned planning of time and we have another two or three minutes left, perhaps we could discuss whether there is any purpose in envisaging cross-examination by the second Defence team, that is, the Defence of Cerkez, for bearing in mind the indictment, and especially count 2, persecution, which is the only one that may have some distant theoretical connection with the accused Cerkez, I should like to ask the Prosecution to tell us whether they see this witness as a witness in the Cerkez case at all, and especially since, in count 2 of the indictment, the persecution count, the charges against Cerkez are limited to the municipalities of Vitez, Busovaca and Novi Travnik. Therefore, even informally, I see no connection with the accused Cerkez. But out of caution, I would like to ask the Prosecution to tell me whether they see this witness having any role in the evidence against Cerkez, because of course it is on that answer that my decision as to whether I would cross-examine or not depends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kovacic, it's really for you to decide what cross-examination to undertake and not to be advised. But no doubt you can have a word with Mr. Lopez-Terres during the adjournment, and he can tell you if there's any reliance placed on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, but I think that the Prosecutor should say what is, and he did it in this paper that he gave us, where he listed the points, but not with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's not something for the Trial Chamber. There are some matters which have to be attended to, one of which is something which you referred to, Mr. Kovacic, involving conversations with Mr. Nice. We ought to deal with that at some stage. There are applications from the Prosecution in relation to various witnesses. We ought to deal with those matters. We have been asked informally about the calendar for September, and the answer is that it depends on other matters to some extent. When they are resolved, we'll let you know as soon as possible. I have very much in mind that we ought to be getting that calendar out, and we'll do so as soon as we can. The other matters we have to finalise are the procedural matters which we've started on a number of occasions and never yet finished. I don't know, Mr. Nice, with that indication as to cross-examination, how you see the rest of the week. We are not sitting Wednesday and Friday afternoons, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I view the rest of the week with some concern, because the cross-examination taken so far with this witness is going to make it difficult, I think, to accommodate the other three witnesses who are here for this week, brought in of course in the hope that we were going to be able to move at some greater speed. I'm also concerned about the fact that the practice we've pursued of returning to procedural matters piecemeal in order always to accommodate witnesses as the priority has its own inconveniences of various kinds and lands up putting the Chamber under pressure to make decisions on procedural matters. Sometimes it may be rather swiftly. What I would propose is that we defer procedural matters at least for another day or so, not least because the statement that is being prepared to summarise the dossier has yet to be completed. It's promised by the end of the week. I can, in passing, deal very swiftly with the matter of the correspondence between myself and Mr. Kovacic. In reality, the correspondence is a letter from me, because I was the only witness to events, and that has now been properly filed together with Mr. Kovacic's two other letters, so it's available as part of the Court record. I don't think you need take any time. It's a matter for the Court whether you want it read out or not, but it's now available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Judge, as to procedural matters, it would help us immensely if we could have at least a day or two to absorb the document that is being drafted as part of the dossier so that we can intelligently look at it and discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll defer that until next week. As to the other matters, it may be helpful if the evidence about the conversation was formalised in some way so that it forms part of the record in due course, and perhaps you can discuss that with Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it has been, if it's been available in written form is sufficient. If you want me to read it out or if Mr. Kovacic does, I'm quite happy to deal with that. Incidentally, I just mention this -- no, I won't mention it in the presence of the witness. I'll try and return to it on another day. There's one other matter I told Ms. Featherstone I would mention to you, but the witness is here and it's probably better dealt with in one minute or 30 seconds, for that's all it will take, after the witness is gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, could you be back tomorrow, please, at 9.45, when we will conclude your evidence? If you would like to go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
